questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: With a view to enhance the aesthetic
appeal of the heritage site, the government
sanctioned a massive renovation budget.
options_hi: With a view to enhance the aesthetic
appeal of the heritage site, the government
sanctioned a massive renovation budget.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “enhance” with “enhancing”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Gerunds after "With a view to"

In English grammar, the phrase "With a view to" is a compound preposition used to express a purpose or intention. Unlike the standard infinitive marker "to" (which is followed by V1), the "to" in this specific phrase is a preposition. A preposition must be followed by a Noun or a Gerund (V{ing} used as a noun).

REMEMBER THE LIST

Use gerund or nouns after these phrases or adjectives: Look forward to, With a view to, In addition to, Pay attention to, Conducive to, Accustomed to, Prone to, Vulnerable to, Addicted to, Devoted to, Indifferent to, Object to, Averse to, Opposed to, (Prefer to) etc

💢 Application to the Given Question

"With a view to enhance the aesthetic appeal..."

In this sentence, "With a view to" functions as a fixed prepositional phrase. Following the grammatical requirement of this phrase, the verb "enhance" must be converted into its gerund form, "enhancing," to serve as the object of the preposition.

Corrected Sentence

With a view to enhancing the aesthetic appeal of the heritage site, the government sanctioned a massive renovation budget.

questions.q_en:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

The new leadership aims to __________ significant changes in the organization’s work culture.
questions.q_hi:
Select the most appropriate phrasal verb to fill in the blank.

The new leadership aims to __________ significant changes in the organization’s work culture.
questions.solution_en:
Explanation: The correct answer is option (2).

English Explanation: “Bring about” means to cause something to happen or to make something occur. In the sentence, the new leadership aims to cause significant changes in the organization’s work culture. Therefore, “bring about” correctly conveys the idea of producing or initiating change. “Bring up” means to raise a topic or to nurture a child. “Bring out” means to reveal, publish, or highlight something. “Bring in” means to introduce or earn something. Since the context refers to causing major changes, “bring about” is the most appropriate fit.

1. Bring up (उठाना / पालन-पोषण करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी विषय को चर्चा में लाना या बच्चे का पालन-पोषण करना।
Example: She brought up an important issue during the meeting. (उसने बैठक में एक महत्वपूर्ण मुद्दा उठाया।)

2. Bring about (उत्पन्न करना / कारण बनना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी परिवर्तन या घटना का कारण बनना।
Example 1: The new education policy is expected to bring about major reforms in the examination system. (नई शिक्षा नीति से परीक्षा प्रणाली में बड़े सुधार होने की उम्मीद है।)
Example 2: Technological advancements have brought about rapid development. (तकनीकी प्रगति ने तेज़ विकास को जन्म दिया है।)

3. Bring out (प्रकट करना / प्रकाशित करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी चीज़ को उजागर करना या प्रकाशित करना।
Example: The author brought out a new novel last month. (लेखक ने पिछले महीने एक नई उपन्यास प्रकाशित की।)

4. Bring in (लाना / आय अर्जित करना)
Meaning in Hindi: किसी चीज़ को अंदर लाना या कमाई करना।
Example: The new product brought in huge profits. (नए उत्पाद ने भारी मुनाफा कमाया।)

questions.q_en:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

The guard said to Prachi, "Move another step and I will shoot you!"
questions.q_hi:
In the following question, a sentence has been given in Direct/Indirect speech. Out of the four alternatives suggested, select the one which best expresses the same sentence in Indirect/Direct speech.

The guard said to Prachi, "Move another step and I will shoot you!"
options_en: The guard threatened Prachi to move another step and he would shoot her.
The guard warned Prachi that if she moved another step, he would shoot her.
The guard forbade Prachi to move another step or he will shoot her.
The guard shouted at Prachi that move another step and he would shoot her.
options_hi: The guard threatened Prachi to move another step and he would shoot her.
The guard warned Prachi that if she moved another step, he would shoot her.
The guard forbade Prachi to move another step or he will shoot her.
The guard shouted at Prachi that move another step and he would shoot her.
questions.solution_en:
The correct answer is Option B: The guard warned Prachi that if she moved another step, he would shoot her.

Why this is unique (Key Points):

  • The Conditional Logic: Even though the original sentence starts with a command ("Move..."), it is actually a conditional threat. In indirect speech, we use "if + she moved" to reflect this logic.

  • Reporting Verb: Using "warned" or "threatened" is essential here to capture the danger expressed in the direct speech.

  • Tense Shift:

    • The implied present "move" shifts to the simple past "moved".

    • The future "will shoot" shifts to the conditional "would shoot".

  • Pronoun Change: The second-person pronoun "you" refers to Prachi, so it changes to "her".

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: My youngest brother, who recently
graduated from the prestigious law school,
he is now practicing in the High Court.
options_hi: My youngest brother, who recently
graduated from the prestigious law school,
he is now practicing in the High Court.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (C) Replace “he is now” with “is now”.

Rule / Concept: The Redundant Subject

a sentence should have only one subject for a single predicate (action). A common error occurs when a noun subject is introduced, followed by a relative clause (like who..., which..., that...), and then a pronoun (like he, she, it) is added before the main verb.

Since the noun at the beginning is already the subject of the main verb, the pronoun is unnecessary and grammatically incorrect.

💢 Application to the Given Question

Let's look at the "skeleton" of the sentence:

"My youngest brother (Subject)... is now practicing (Verb)."

Now, look at how the error is inserted:

"My youngest brother (A), who recently graduated from (B) the prestigious law school, he is now (C)..."

  1. The subject is "My youngest brother".

  2. The phrase "who recently graduated... school" is an adjective clause giving more info about the brother.

  3. The word "he" is a pronoun referring back to the brother.

Because "My youngest brother" is already waiting to perform the action "is practicing," adding "he" creates a Double Subject. You must delete the pronoun.

Corrected Sentence "My youngest brother, who recently graduated from the prestigious law school, is now practicing in the High Court."

questions.q_en:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.

The regulatory body is believed to have completed the inspection before issuing the clearance certificate.
questions.q_hi:
Select the passive form of the given sentence.

The regulatory body is believed to have completed the inspection before issuing the clearance certificate.
options_en: The inspection is believed to be completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection is believed to have been completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection was believed to have completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection is being believed to have been completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
options_hi: The inspection is believed to be completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection is believed to have been completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection was believed to have completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
The inspection is being believed to have been completed before issuing the clearance certificate.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B).

📌 Rule / Concept: Perfect Infinitive in Passive (to have been + V³)

When an active sentence contains a reporting verb followed by a perfect infinitive structure — is believed to have + V³ — and the action needs to be converted into passive, the structure must change to:

Subject + is/was + believed/said/expected + to have been + V³

The word “been” is mandatory in perfect passive infinitive constructions. The structure becomes:

to have been + past participle (V³)

Without “been,” the sentence remains in active sense. Here:

“is believed” = reporting passive
“to have completed” = perfect infinitive (active)
Object = “the inspection”

To convert into passive, “the inspection” must become the subject, and “to have completed” must become “to have been completed.”

questions.q_en: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
questions.q_hi: Select the sentence that is grammatically correct.
options_en: The jury were unanimous in its decision to appoint a new chairman.
Neither the principal nor the teachers was present at the meeting.
The Prime Minister, rather than his cabinet colleagues, has the final authority.
No one in the building, except for the security guards, were aware of the fire.
options_hi: The jury were unanimous in its decision to appoint a new chairman.
Neither the principal nor the teachers was present at the meeting.
The Prime Minister, rather than his cabinet colleagues, has the final authority.
No one in the building, except for the security guards, were aware of the fire.
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is - Option (C)- This sentence correctly applies the First Subject Priority rule.

Rule/Concept: Rule of "Rather than" When subjects are joined by "rather than," the verb ignores the second subject and agrees strictly with the first subject.

Why the other options are INCORRECT

Sentence (A)- Collective Noun Inconsistency

The Trap: Using a plural verb "were" with a singular pronoun "its".

The Rule: "Unanimous" implies the group is acting as one unit. It requires a singular verb (was) and a singular pronoun (its).

Correction: The jury was unanimous in its decision...

Sentence (B)- The Proximity Rule Trap

The Trap: The student might try to apply the "First Subject" rule here, but "Neither... nor" follows a different logic.

The Rule: For Neither... nor, the verb must agree with the nearest subject. Here, the nearest subject is "teachers" (plural).

Correction: Neither the principal nor the teachers were present...

Sentence (D)- "Except" vs. Indefinite Pronoun

The Trap: The plural "security guards" tempts the student to use "were".

The Rule: "Except" is a qualifier. The verb must agree with the first subject, "No one," which is always singular.

Correction: No one... except for the guards... was aware...

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: Despite his busy schedule,
our manager goes seldom to
the gym in the evening.
No Error
options_hi: Despite his busy schedule,
our manager goes seldom to
the gym in the evening.
No Error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (B) Replace “goes seldom to” with “seldom goes to”.

Rule / Concept: Position of Adverb of Frequency

Indefinite adverb of frequency(often, seldom, always, rarely, never etc.)

Before main verb

Definite adverb of frequency(daily, weekly, monthly, yearly etc.):-

At the end of the clause/sentence

At both positions:- Regularly, frequently, occasionally etc

Application to the Given Question

"...our manager goes seldom to the gym in the evening."

In this sentence, "goes" is the main verb. According to the rule, the adverb of frequency "seldom" must be placed before the main verb

Corrected Sentence

Despite his busy schedule, our manager seldom goes to the gym in the evening.

More Examples for Clarity

Example 1: He always arrives on time. (Before Main Verb) ✅

Example 2: She is often busy on Mondays. (After 'Be' Verb) ✅

Example 3: They have never visited Paris. (Between Auxiliary and Main Verb) ✅

Incorrect Usage

Wrong example 1: He arrives always on time. ❌

Wrong example 2: She often is busy on Mondays. ❌

Things to Remember / Exam Tips

  • The "Main Verb" Anchor: Identify the action. If it's a single main verb (like eats, plays, goes), the adverb goes in front of it.

  • The "Be" Exception: If the verb is is, am, are, was, or were, the adverb must follow it (e.g., "He is never late," NOT "He never is late").

  • Negative Adverbs: Words like seldom, rarely, and never are already negative; do not use another negative word (like not) with them.

questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “has to” with “had to”.

📌 Rule / Concept: Narrative Tense Consistency (Modal Verbs)

In English, when a sentence describes a specific event that happened in the past, all related verbs and modals must reflect that past timeframe.

  • Present Obligation: Has to / Have to

  • Past Obligation: Had to



If the trigger for an action is written in the Simple Past (e.g., noticed), the resulting action must also be expressed in a past form. Using "has to" (Present) implies a general rule or a current requirement, which contradicts the specific past incident described in the rest of the sentence.



💢 Application to the Given Question

"A London-bound train has to stop... when the conductor noticed smoke..."

The sentence describes a specific incident:

  1. The Trigger: The conductor noticed smoke ($V_2$ - Simple Past).

  2. The Result: The train has to stop (Present).

Because the conductor noticed the smoke in the past, the "necessity" to stop the train also occurred in the past. Therefore, the present modal "has to" must be converted to the past modal "had to" to maintain logical consistency throughout the narrative.

Corrected Sentence

A London-bound train had to stop at a remote station when the conductor noticed smoke rising from one of the rear coaches during the journey.

📌 Rule / Concept: Simple Past Tense – Active to Passive Conversion

In the Simple Past tense, the active structure is:
Subject + V² + Object

The passive structure becomes:

Object + was/were + V³ (+ by + Subject)

The auxiliary verb (was/were) must agree with the new subject, and the main verb must be in past participle (V³) form.

Here, “sanctioned” is in Simple Past tense.
“The emergency funds” is the object and becomes the subject in passive voice. Since it is plural, the correct auxiliary is “were”. The verb “sanctioned” remains in V³ form.

Hence, “were sanctioned” is the correct transformation.

Whoever submitted the anonymous complaint to the authorities clearly possessed detailed knowledge of the internal operations of the company.
questions.q_hi:
In the sentence below, identify the type of pronoun of the word “whoever”:

Whoever submitted the anonymous complaint to the authorities clearly possessed detailed knowledge of the internal operations of the company.
questions.solution_en:
Answer: D) Indefinite Pronoun

Explanation: An indefinite pronoun refers to a person or thing in a non-specific or indefinite way.

Words like someone, anyone, everybody, whoever, and whatever are indefinite pronouns.

Here, “whoever” does not refer to any particular person. It means “any person who.”

Therefore, “whoever” is an indefinite pronoun.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: The committee members
have unanimously elected
the Mr. Sharma the President
of the association for the upcoming term.
options_hi: The committee members
have unanimously elected
the Mr. Sharma the President
of the association for the upcoming term.
questions.solution_en:
Correction: Replace “the Mr. Sharma the President” with “Mr. Sharma President”.

Rule/Concept: Omission of Articles with Titles and Appointments –

The definite article 'the' is omitted before a noun that serves as a complement or is used in apposition to a person’s name, especially after verbs like elect, appoint, make, crown, or choose. Additionally, articles are never used before titles like Mr., Mrs., Sir, or Lord when followed by a proper name.

Application to the Given Question-

Error 1: The use of "the" before "Mr. Sharma" is incorrect. Honorifics do not take articles.

Error 2: The use of "the" before "President" is incorrect here because "President" is the objective complement of the verb "elected". When you elect someone to a position, the position title loses its article.

Corrected Sentence "The committee members have unanimously elected Mr. Sharma President of the association for the upcoming term."

More Examples for Clarity-

They appointed him Chairman. (Not: the Chairman)

We made him Captain of our team. (Not: the Captain)

Corrected Sentence "The committee members have unanimously elected Mr. Sharma President of the association for the upcoming term."

Things to Remember / Exam Tips-

The "Verb" Trigger: Watch out for Elect, Appoint, Nominate, Make. If you see these, check if the title following them has an unnecessary "the".

Title + Name: Remember, it's "Queen Elizabeth", not "The Queen Elizabeth".

The Present Subjunctive is used in "that-clauses" following nouns that express a formal command, decree, or necessity (such as decree, mandate, order, requirement, suggestion). In this mood, the verb in the following clause must be in its base form (the infinitive without "to"), regardless of whether the subject is singular or plural.

In the indicative mood, "evacuates" would be correct; however, because a formal decree is being expressed, the subjunctive base form evacuate must be used. The length of the subject ("every citizen residing in the low-lying coastal areas") is designed to distract you from this rule.

questions.q_en: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
questions.q_hi: The following sentence has been split into four segments. Identify the segment that contains a grammatical error.
options_en: They were luckily not travelling
in the train which met
with an accident last night.
No error
options_hi: They were luckily not travelling
in the train which met
with an accident last night.
No error
questions.solution_en:
The Correct Ans is Option (A) Replace “They were luckily” with “Luckily, they were”

Concept: Placement of "Sentence Adverbs"

There are certain adverbs (like luckily, fortunately, happily, surprisingly, honestly) that modify the entire sentence or the speaker’s attitude toward the situation, rather than just the verb. These are called Sentence Adverbs.

  • Rule: When an adverb modifies the whole sentence, it should ideally be placed at the very beginning of the sentence, followed by a comma.

  • The Trap: If you place "luckily" after the verb "were," it suggests that the manner of their being was lucky, which is awkward. We want to say that the entire situation (them not being on the train) was a piece of good luck.

Application to the Given Question

The sentence describes a fortunate escape from a train accident. The "luck" doesn't apply to the action of traveling; it applies to the fact that they happened to be elsewhere.

  • Incorrect: They were luckily not travelling... (This incorrectly tries to modify the verb phrase).

  • Correct: Luckily, they were not travelling... (This modifies the whole fact that they weren't on the train).

Corrected Sentence

Luckily, they were not travelling in the train which met with an accident last night.

More Examples for Clarity

  1. Fortunately: Fortunately, the fire was extinguished before it reached the kitchen.

  2. Honestly: Honestly, I don't know the answer to your question.

  3. Surprisingly: Surprisingly, the team won despite having no experience.
